title: Functions: domain, range and inverse (informal)

points.text: What makes a relation a function; domain, range, graph and function notation
Functions as models of real situations
An inverse undoes a function; its graph is the reflection in y=x

bigPicture: A function gives exactly one output per input. Its domain (allowed inputs) and range (outputs) matter as much as the rule; an inverse runs the function backwards.

keyIdeas.cue: When is a relation a function?
keyIdeas.answer: Each x in the domain maps to exactly one y (vertical-line test).

keyIdeas.cue: Why do models restrict the domain?
keyIdeas.answer: Inputs must make sense in context, e.g. time t ≥ 0, number of items n ∈ ℕ.

keyIdeas.cue: How are the graphs of f and f⁻¹ related?
keyIdeas.answer: Reflections in y = x; domain of f⁻¹ = range of f.

misconceptions.right: The −1 is notation for inverse, not a power.

practice.prompt: f(x) = 1/(x − 3) + 2. Write down the largest possible domain and the range.
Sketch y = f(x) = x³ + 1 and y = f⁻¹(x) on the same axes for −2 ≤ x ≤ 2, showing the line y = x.
practice.answer: Two curves symmetric about y = x

assessmentNote: AA SL external exams: Paper 1 without a calculator and Paper 2 with a GDC, both written answers in sections A (short) and B (extended); no multiple choice. Practice prompts here are original and are not predictions of exam questions.

memorise: Vertical-line test; domain of f⁻¹ = range of f
Usual domain exclusions: division by 0, even root of negative, log of non-positive
